title: Thyroid nodule and differentiated thyroid cancer
subject: surgery
summary: Work up a thyroid nodule, tell papillary from follicular cancer, and manage and follow up DTC the way exams and current practice expect.

objectives.text: Choose the first investigation for a solitary thyroid nodule, and say when a scan is needed and which test answers 'what is the nodule'
Tell how papillary carcinoma is diagnosed (nuclear features) from how follicular carcinoma is diagnosed (invasion on histology), and say what FNAC or frozen section can and cannot settle
Pick the thyroid cancer that is most common overall, in children, after radiation, in a thyroglossal cyst and in iodine deficiency, and name its commonest mutation
Tell the usual route and sites of spread of papillary versus follicular carcinoma, and exclude medullary and anaplastic from DTC
Choose the action for each Bethesda category, separating II from IV and V
Choose the extent of surgery for a given DTC (lobectomy versus total thyroidectomy), giving both the classic key and current practice
Decide who needs radioiodine, how TSH is raised before ablation, and how long-term TSH suppression is matched to risk
Pick the follow-up marker for DTC versus medullary carcinoma, and interpret thyroglobulin with antibodies and a negative radioiodine scan
Identify the commonest complication after thyroidectomy, match voice and airway changes to the nerve injured, and choose the first step for a neck haematoma
State the AJCC staging age cut-off and place the look-alikes (oncocytic, microcarcinoma, prognosis) correctly

traps.trap: FNAC is the first investigation for a solitary thyroid nodule (merges TR2: radionuclide scan first)
Follicular carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer
Cytology or frozen section can diagnose follicular carcinoma
Papillary carcinoma is diagnosed by its papillary architecture (merges TR9: psammoma bodies are PTC-exclusive)
An encapsulated follicular variant of PTC is a carcinoma
The AJCC age cut-off for DTC staging is 45 years
Total thyroidectomy is the treatment for all differentiated thyroid cancer (merges TR19: one size cut-off)
A lateral aberrant thyroid is ectopic thyroid tissue
Papillary spreads by blood and follicular spreads by lymphatics
Cervical lymph nodes are the usual site of follicular carcinoma spread (merges TR13: medullary and anaplastic counted as DTC)
A negative radioiodine scan rules out recurrence when thyroglobulin is raised
Radioiodine is given to every DTC patient
Bethesda II nodule needs surgery
Bethesda IV and V mean the same management
Loss of high-pitched voice is recurrent laryngeal nerve injury
The most common complication after thyroidectomy is nerve injury or bleeding
A neck haematoma is first managed by reintubation
TSH should be suppressed before radioiodine ablation (merges TR17: one TSH target for every risk group)
A low thyroglobulin is reassuring when anti-thyroglobulin antibodies are present
Calcitonin is the marker for differentiated thyroid cancer

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

That choice is not right. It tempts because older exam papers keyed FNAC as the first test, and FNAC is the test that judges what a nodule is.
But 'first' and 'best for the nature of the nodule' are different questions. Ask what must be known before a needle goes in.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the verb in the stem: the exam key and current practice differ on this exact word, 'first'.

say.text: That choice is not right. A radionuclide scan tempts because it sorts a nodule into hot or cold, which sounds like a good first split.

say.text: A low TSH points to the nodule's function. Which test looks at function, and does it need a needle?
That choice is not right. FNAC tempts because it is the test for the nature of a nodule, so it feels like the next step whatever the TSH shows.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so notice that the old key is talking. A low TSH changes the question.

sure_note.text: You were sure, but a needle is chosen by the result, not by habit.

say.text: Yes. A low TSH sends you to a radionuclide scan, which looks for a hot, hyperfunctioning nodule.
A hot nodule is rarely malignant, so FNAC is not the first step for it.
A cold nodule, one that does not take up iodine, carries a higher risk than a hot one, but most cold nodules are still benign.
So the scan sorts hot from cold. A cold nodule that looks suspicious on ultrasound is the one that needs FNAC.
Ultrasound is the second filter. Suspicious features include hypoechogenicity, microcalcifications, a taller-than-wide shape and irregular margins.
Only about 5 to 15 percent of nodules are malignant, which is why the filters keep most patients away from needles.
FNAC is reported as Bethesda IV, a follicular neoplasm. The surgeon asks whether this is carcinoma.
Which test settles it?

choices.label: Frozen section of the nodule during surgery
Histology of the resected lobe for invasion
Repeat FNAC with a finer ultrasound needle
Not sure, give me a hint

That choice is not right. It tempts because FNAC judges the nature of the nodule, so a better needle feels like a better answer.

say.text: That choice is not right. A frozen section sounds like a quick histology answer, which is why it tempts you.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Frozen section is histology, but it does not settle a follicular lesion.

say.text: Yes. Follicular carcinoma is diagnosed only by capsular or vascular invasion on histology.
FNAC can report the lesion as Bethesda IV but cannot separate adenoma from carcinoma.

choices.label: Capsular or vascular invasion on histology

say.text: That choice is not right. A follicular pattern looks like the diagnosis on a smear, which is why it tempts you.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Calcitonin points to one cell line, so match the marker to its cancer before you use it.

say.text: Yes. Routine thyroglobulin is not useful for diagnosing a nodule before surgery, so FNAC and histology do the diagnosing.
Calcitonin is raised in medullary carcinoma, not in DTC, and thyroglobulin is the follow-up marker of DTC.

choices.label: Papillae with fibrovascular cores, seen at low power

Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The name describes the shape of the groups. Ask what the pathologist checks inside each cell at high power.
That choice is not right. Papillae are real, and the name comes from them, so they feel diagnostic.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one matters: architecture is the easiest feature to see, which is why it misleads.

say.text: That choice is not right. Psammoma bodies are a real papillary feature, so they tempt you as a sign that settles the call.
But they are often present and only supportive. They also occur in serous ovarian tumours, meningioma and mesothelioma.
Right. Papillary carcinoma is diagnosed on its nuclei: optically clear, ground-glass nuclei with grooves and pseudoinclusions.
The papillae are the architecture the name suggests, but the diagnosis rests on the nuclear features.

say.text: Ask which tissue shows a whole capsule, and whether the pathologist can see a capsule being crossed on a slide of cells.
That choice is not right. More material feels like a better answer, so a finer needle tempts you.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is the key idea: cytology reports the cells, and the diagnosis needs the tissue.

say.text: That choice is not right. A frozen section feels like a quick answer during surgery, so it tempts you.

Right. Follicular carcinoma is diagnosed only by capsular or vascular invasion, which needs histology. Cytology alone cannot make it.

say.text: That choice is not right. A capsule is what makes many follicular tumours look benign, so it tempts you to call this an adenoma.

K128.text: Tumour marker for follow-up of DTC — Serum thyroglobulin (with anti-Tg antibodies)

K129.text: Tumour marker for medullary carcinoma — Calcitonin (and CEA)

K130.text: Most common complication after total thyroidectomy — Hypocalcaemia (transient hypoparathyroidism)

K131.text: Treatment of choice for most DTC needing surgery (classic answer) — Total thyroidectomy

K134.text: PYQs have expected **FNAC** as "the first investigation" for a solitary thyroid nodule; current guideline practice is **TSH and ultrasound first**, with FNAC as the investigation of choice for the nature of the nodule.

K135.text: PYQs have expected **total thyroidectomy** for all DTC; current ATA guidance accepts **lobectomy** for low-risk tumours of 1–4 cm and lobectomy or active surveillance for low-risk microcarcinoma.

K136.text: PYQs have expected an age cut-off of **45 years** in DTC staging; the current AJCC 8th edition uses **55 years**.

K138.text: PYQs have treated the **encapsulated follicular variant of PTC** as cancer; since 2016 the non-invasive form is called **NIFTP** and is not a carcinoma.

K139.text: Exam keys pair **psammoma bodies with PTC**; they also occur in serous ovarian tumours, meningioma and mesothelioma, which may appear as distractors.

cards.q: What are the first tests for a solitary thyroid nodule, and what does FNAC answer?
cards.a: Serum TSH and neck ultrasound come first. Ultrasound-guided FNAC is the test of choice for the nature of the nodule; a scan follows only if TSH is low.

cards.q: How is papillary carcinoma diagnosed, and how is follicular carcinoma diagnosed?
cards.a: Papillary: nuclear features (optically clear nuclei, grooves, pseudoinclusions). Follicular: capsular or vascular invasion on histology; FNAC cannot do it.

cards.q: Which thyroid cancer is most common overall, and which rises in iodine deficiency?
cards.a: Papillary carcinoma overall, about 80–85%. Follicular carcinoma rises in relative share in iodine-deficient areas.

cards.q: Usual route and sites of spread of papillary versus follicular carcinoma?
cards.a: Papillary spreads by lymphatics to neck nodes. Follicular spreads by blood to lung and bone, with nodes uncommon.

cards.q: Action for Bethesda II and for Bethesda IV?
cards.a: Bethesda II: clinical and ultrasound follow-up, surgery only for compression or cosmesis. Bethesda IV: diagnostic lobectomy or molecular testing.

cards.q: Extent of surgery for a low-risk DTC of 1–4 cm?
cards.a: Lobectomy or total thyroidectomy are both acceptable under ATA 2015; the PYQ key expected total thyroidectomy.

cards.q: When is radioiodine given, and what TSH is needed before a dose?
cards.a: Not routinely for ATA low-risk disease; recommended for high-risk and metastatic disease. A dose needs a high TSH, from withdrawal or recombinant TSH.

cards.q: Which marker follows DTC after total thyroidectomy, and what must be checked with it?
cards.a: Serum thyroglobulin, read only with anti-thyroglobulin antibodies negative and alongside neck ultrasound. Calcitonin is the marker for medullary carcinoma.

cards.q: Commonest complication after total thyroidectomy, and first step for a tense neck haematoma?
cards.a: Transient hypocalcaemia from parathyroid hypofunction. A tense neck haematoma: open the wound at the bedside first, then secure the airway.

E1.text: You tend to confuse look-alikes: papillary architecture for papillary nuclei, or one laryngeal nerve for another. Before answering, name the one feature that separates the pair.

E2.text: You tend to add familiar items to a set, such as nodes to follicular spread or any thyroid cancer to DTC. Rebuild the set from its logic, then test each item against it.

E3.text: You tend to reverse a mechanism: spread routes or the TSH direction around radioiodine. Predict from the cause first, such as invasion of vessels meaning blood spread, then check.

E4.text: You tend to stretch 'most common' to mean the most dramatic. Read the exact qualifier: commonest, most feared and first-line are different questions.

E5.text: You tend to answer with the older PYQ key where current practice differs: FNAC first, total thyroidectomy for all, age 45, any follicular variant as cancer. Hold both: what PYQs expected and what is current.

E6.text: You tend to swap adjacent numbers or categories. Tie each number to its word and its action, then test yourself on the word first.

E7.text: You tend to miss the qualifier: iodine-deficient versus sufficient, low versus high risk, or antibodies present. Underline the qualifier in the stem before reading the options.

E8.text: You tend to pick a test that cannot answer the question asked: cytology for invasion, or a repeat scan for refractory disease. Ask what each test can see, then climb the ladder.

E9.text: You tend to get the order wrong: operating on a benign report or intubating before releasing a clot. Ask what comes first and why before choosing.

E10.text: You tend to pair a name or marker with the wrong condition: lateral aberrant thyroid as ectopia, or calcitonin with DTC. Pair by site and cell of origin instead of by label.
